lead: Ruby and He-Ne were the first lasers built, and they still show the two basic pumping routes. Ruby is a sapphire crystal (Al₂O₃) holding a small fraction of Cr³⁺ ions; a flashlamp drives a three-level cycle and the output is a short red pulse at 694.3 nm. He-Ne is a gas mixture in a discharge tube; collisions hand energy from helium to neon, giving a continuous red beam at 632.8 nm. Both beams are red, so their numbers are easy to swap under exam pressure. Only a few universities teach this pair in detail.
prereq: You need 5.1 photon energy and stimulated emission and 5.2 population inversion, pumping and the optical cavity.

blocks.text: Ruby is aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃, sapphire) doped with about 0.05 % chromium. The Cr³⁺ ions give the pink colour and do all the lasing. A rod a few centimetres long sits between two mirrors, one fully silvered and one partly silvered, so light passes through the rod many times.

items: The flashlamp fires a bright white flash; Cr³⁺ ions absorb green and blue light and rise from the ground level to broad pump bands.
Fast non-radiative decay drops them to the metastable level, which lives about 3 ms, so ions collect there.
Pumping is strong enough that the metastable level holds more ions than the ground level: population inversion, because the laser transition ends at the ground level.
A passing 694.3 nm photon triggers stimulated emission; the ion falls straight to the ground level and the light is amplified.
The pulse escapes through the partial mirror as a short, high-energy red flash. A second flash repeats the cycle.

blocks.text: The lower laser level is the ground level itself. More than half of all Cr³⁺ ions must be lifted before gain appears, so the pump must be violent. That is why ruby is a three-level, pulsed laser: a flashlamp cannot fire continuously without overheating the rod.

sections.h3: He-Ne: energy transfer in a gas

blocks.text: The tube holds helium and neon in roughly 10:1 ratio at a few torr, with a DC discharge of about 1 kV. Helium does the absorbing; neon does the lasing.

items: Electron collisions in the discharge excite helium atoms into long-lived metastable states.
A metastable helium atom strikes a ground-state neon atom. The two energy levels nearly match, so energy transfers resonantly and neon is left in its 3s level.
The neon 3s → 2p transition emits 632.8 nm, amplified between the mirrors.
The neon 2p level empties quickly by spontaneous emission to the 1s level, and helium returns to ground at the tube walls.

blocks.text: Because the lower level (2p) clears itself, the inversion needs only a modest pump, and the beam is continuous: a few milliwatts at 632.8 nm with a very narrow linewidth. Compare the two: ruby gives joule pulses at 694.3 nm, He-Ne gives milliwatts steady at 632.8 nm.

figure.caption: The left chain is the ruby three-level cycle: emission returns ions to the ground level, so the laser must run in pulses. The right chain is He-Ne: metastable helium hands energy to neon, whose lower level empties fast enough for continuous output.

spec.title: Ruby cycle and He-Ne transfer
spec.aria: Two vertical chains: ruby runs from Cr³⁺ ground level through pump bands and the metastable level to a 694.3 nm pulse that returns to ground; He-Ne runs from the discharge through helium metastable and neon 3s and 2p levels to a 632.8 nm continuous output.

examples.question: A ruby laser emits a 1.0 J pulse at 694.3 nm. Find the energy of one photon and the number of photons in the pulse. Take h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s.
steps: Convert the wavelength to metres: λ = 694.3 nm = 694.3 × 10⁻⁹ m = 6.943×10⁻⁷ m.
Number of photons N = pulse energy ÷ photon energy = 1.0 J ÷ 2.864×10⁻¹⁹ J.
examples.answer: Each photon carries 2.864×10⁻¹⁹ J, so a 1.0 J pulse contains 3.49×10¹⁸ photons.
examples.check:
h = 6.63e-34
c = 3.00e8
lam = 694.3e-9
E = h * c / lam
N = 1.0 / E
print(f"{E:.3e}")
print(f"{N:.2e}")

traps: Ruby is three-level and pulsed. Its laser transition ends at the ground state, so more than half the ions must be pumped; it never runs continuously.
Keep the reds apart: ruby is 694.3 nm, He-Ne is 632.8 nm. A question that says only 'red laser' is testing this.
In He-Ne the lasing atom is neon. Helium only absorbs discharge energy and passes it on by collision.
Ruby gives joule pulses, He-Ne gives milliwatts. Do not plug a ruby pulse energy into a continuous-power formula.
Ruby inversion is between the metastable level and the ground level, not between two excited levels.

quiz.q: Which ion lases in a ruby laser, and in which host crystal?
quiz.a: Cr³⁺ ions in an Al₂O₃ (sapphire) crystal.

quiz.q: State the output wavelength and operating mode of the ruby and He-Ne lasers.
quiz.a: Ruby: 694.3 nm, pulsed. He-Ne: 632.8 nm, continuous.

quiz.q: Why must a ruby laser be operated in pulses?
quiz.a: The laser transition ends at the ground level, so more than half of all Cr³⁺ ions must be excited before inversion exists. That needs a very strong flashlamp, which heats the rod; so it fires in short pulses only.

quiz.q: What is helium's role in a He-Ne laser?
quiz.a: The discharge excites helium into metastable states. A metastable helium atom collides with a ground-state neon atom and transfers its energy, leaving neon in the 3s level. Helium does not lase.

quiz.q: A He-Ne laser gives 1.0 mW at 632.8 nm. Find the number of photons emitted per second.
Using their level schemes, explain why He-Ne needs a small pump for continuous output while ruby needs a huge pulsed pump.
quiz.a: Ruby's lower level is the ground level, which is always full, so at least half the ions must be lifted before gain appears; only a flashlamp can do that, and only in bursts. In He-Ne the lower level (2p) is emptied by fast spontaneous decay, so it stays nearly empty; a small inversion is enough and a modest DC discharge sustains it continuously.

beyond: Not for the exam. He-Ne tubes once sat inside every supermarket barcode scanner; diode lasers have replaced them almost everywhere. Ruby's three-level cycle survives as the standard first model of a laser threshold, and the same 'lower level must empty fast' argument decides whether any new medium can run continuous wave. Next, look up the actual neon term symbols (3s₂ and 2p₄) and why the 632.8 nm line wins over the competing 1.15 μm and 3.39 μm lines.
